member.name: T:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory
member.summary: The Iris production app's composition root. Wires the Blazor Web App, the ActivityPub server (via Iris.Server's AddActivityPubServer / MapActivityPubEndpoints, unchanged), in-memory persistence, and the single seeded local actor, then builds the application. Exposed as a public seam so the integration tests (Iris.Web.Tests) can boot the identical host in-process (via ) against a TestServer.

remarks.para: Slice 32.1 is the bare host: it proves the library's federation endpoints (WebFinger, actor document, inbox, outbox) work inside the new Blazor Web App process, before production persistence (32.2), local auth (32.3), and the product screens (32.4) are layered on. The composition order follows docs/plans/production-app-web-host-structure.md §2: Razor components first, then the ActivityPub server, then the app pipeline (signature validation + ActivityPub endpoints, then the Razor component endpoints).

The host binds to http://localhost:8088 by default (the production port, see production-app-overview.md §2 — the reverse proxy for https://iris.luit.ink targets host 8088). The advertised base URI defaults to http://localhost:8088 too; an operator sets Iris:AdvertiseBase to expose the instance under a public hostname while listening elsewhere.

member.name: F:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.DefaultMaxRequestBodySize
member.summary: The default cap on an inbound HTTP request body, in bytes (1 MiB). ActivityPub federation payloads (an activity JSON document) are small — well under a few tens of KB in practice — so a 1 MiB ceiling is generous for legitimate traffic. It exists to bound the memory an **unauthenticated** inbound POST /ap/v1/u/{handle}/inbox can force the app to buffer: without it, Kestrel's default (no request-body limit) lets a malicious peer stream an arbitrarily large body into memory (a denial-of-service vector for a public instance). An operator raises it via Iris:MaxRequestBodySize (env IRIS_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_SIZE) if a legitimate use case (e.g. very large embedded media on an activity) requires it.

member.name: F:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.MaxRequestBodySizeConfigKey
member.summary: The configuration key for the inbound request-body size cap (see ). Bound from Iris:MaxRequestBodySize.

member.name: F:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.DefaultShutdownDrainTimeout
member.summary: The default host-shutdown delivery drain budget (slice 33.6): how long the DeliveryWorker gets, once the host's stopping token is cancelled (a SIGTERM), to finish its in-flight outbound deliveries before it stops. The host itself stops after HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout (30 s by default, set by WebApplicationBuilder's default) — and that 30 s covers every hosted service in registration order (the EF persistence provider's StopAsync runs before the delivery worker's), so a 60 s worker drain budget would be truncated by the host's own timeout. The default is therefore 15 s: comfortably above the seconds-scale delivery round-trips it protects, and comfortably below the 30 s host budget, so the worker always returns before the host force-stops it. An operator raises it via Iris:Delivery:ShutdownDrainTimeout (env IRIS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT) when its delivery traffic (or a busy queue) needs a longer drain — and should then also raise DOTNET_HOST__SHUTDOWNTIMEOUT so the host's own budget covers it.

member.name: F:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.ShutdownDrainTimeoutConfigKey
member.summary: The configuration key for the host-shutdown delivery drain budget (slice 33.6). Bound from Iris:Delivery:ShutdownDrainTimeout (env IRIS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT); the value is a string (e.g. "00:00:30") or a number of seconds (e.g. "30"). Unset → .

When no origins are configured, no policy is registered and no CORS middleware runs, so the app is same-origin-only by default (the safe default for a public instance).

member.name: F:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.EnableAntiforgeryConfigKey
member.summary: The configuration key that toggles ASP.NET Core antiforgery validation (Phase 94). Bound from Iris:Security:EnableAntiforgery (env IRIS_SECURITY_ENABLEANTIFORGERY). When unset or any non-false value, antiforgery validation is enabled (the production default — login/register form POSTs are validated against a per-session token). Set to false (case-insensitive) to disable validation: a PermissiveAntiforgery (a no-op IAntiforgery) is registered so the UseAntiforgery middleware's IsRequestValidAsync always passes, and POSTs go through without a valid token. The middleware itself is always applied (the endpoints carry antiforgery metadata, so removing it would throw); only the token check is turned off. This exists for development / Playwright testing, where a stale antiforgery token (one signed with a previous Data Protection key ring, e.g. after a container rebuild) would otherwise make the login/register forms fail with a 400 until the token is re-fetched. When disabled, the /local/v1/antiforgery token-issuance endpoint still works (the client can fetch a token harmlessly).

member.name: F:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.DevCacheBypassConfigKey
member.summary: The configuration key that toggles development cache bypass (Phase 131.6). Bound from Iris:Dev:CacheBypass (env IRIS_DEV_CACHEBYPASS). When true (case-insensitive), the SPA shell (index.html) is served with Cache-Control: no-store and CSS/JS static assets with Cache-Control: no-cache (revalidated on every request), so a browser never serves a stale build after a container redeploy — the recurring "the site is stuck on an old version" pain during active development. The fingerprinted /_framework/ WASM assets are cached long-term (max-age=31536000, immutable) in BOTH modes: they are content-hashed per build, so a redeploy changes their URLs and they are safe to cache aggressively regardless.
member.remarks: The C# production default is false (cache normally — correct for a public instance). The development compose stack defaults it to true (env IRIS_DEV_CACHEBYPASS, override back to false to restore normal caching), mirroring the antiforgery dev-default pattern. Unset/blank or any non-true value → cache normally (fail closed to production behavior, so a misconfiguration can never accidentally serve an uncached, slower site to public users).

member.name: M:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.ResolveShellVersion(System.String)
member.summary: Resolves the per-build version stamp for the WASM shell's fixed-URL tags (Phase 137.x): a short content hash of the published _framework/ payload the server is actually serving, or null when the directory is absent or empty (the shell is then served un-stamped, with the no-cache header still protecting against a stale shell).
member.param: The server's web root (where the WASM _framework/ output lives).
member.remarks: The stamp is derived from the payload on disk, not from an assembly attribute: the Blazor WebAssembly SDK's PublishTrimmed output has no plain Iris.Web.Client.dll (the main assembly is the content-hashed Iris.Web.Client.{hash}.wasm), so there is no stable file to read a version from. Instead, the stamp is a SHA-256 over the sorted (name, size) of every asset under _framework/, prefixed with the app's Major.Minor.Build. The asset names are themselves content-hashed per build (each file is <assembly>.<hash>.<ext>), so the set of names changes whenever the WASM payload changes; the size is folded in as a belt-and-braces signal so a content change is caught even in the (unlikely) case it left every name unchanged. The result is stable across identical rebuilds and distinct across different builds — exactly the property a cache-bust key needs. It is computed once per host start (the _framework/ directory does not change for the life of a running server), so the per-request shell rewrite is a cheap in-memory string operation.

member.name: M:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.StampShellVersion(System.String,System.String)
member.summary:
Stamps the WASM shell's fixed-URL tags with a per-build query string (Phase 137.x), so a redeploy gives the browser a fresh URL for the loader script, the app stylesheet, and the app's js/*.js files instead of a stale cached copy. Rewrites:
<script src="_framework/..."> → src="_framework/...?v={version}"
relative <link href="...css"> / <script src="...js"> → the same ?v={version} suffix (absolute and favicon URLs are left alone).
Idempotent: an already-stamped URL is re-stamped (the previous ?v= is replaced), so a shell that was stamped at an earlier build (e.g. a leftover wwwroot) converges on the current version rather than accumulating suffixes. A null version returns the content unchanged.

member.name: M:Iris.Web.WebAppFactory.NormalizeLocalActorPemLineEndings(Iris.Server.Stores.IPersistenceProvider,Iris.Core.Identity.Iri)
member.summary: Normalizes CRLF → LF line endings in the publicKeyPem of every local actor (one-time, idempotent repair, 157). Before 138.11 the PEM emitter produced CRLF (RFC 4648); a peer that resolves a key from an actor's publicKeyPem — and that rejects CRLF (Lemmy's deserializer, and the mastodon/hachyderm class that gates actor-doc GETs behind a resolvable key) — could not parse such a PEM, so it rejected the instance's signed requests and the two instances deadlocked in mutual key resolution. The 138.11 fix made the emitter LF-only, but it only re-stamps actors the seed re-stores on boot; actors provisioned at signup (the registration flow) are not re-stamped, so the instance signer (e.g. a registered account set as InstanceActorId) could keep serving a stale CRLF PEM indefinitely.
member.remarks: This walks every stored actor and, for each local actor (IRI prefix matches ) whose publicKeyPem contains a CRLF, replaces every \r\n with \n and re-persists the document. The fix is a pure line-ending normalization (the base64 key payload — and therefore the public key identity — is unchanged), so no key material is re-derived and no relationship is disturbed. Remote cached actors (IRIs not under the instance base) are never touched: their PEM belongs to the remote instance. The method is a no-op once every local actor's PEM is LF-only.
member.param: The persistence provider (provides the ).
The instance base IRI (e.g. https://iris.luit.ink); local actors are those whose IRI starts with this prefix.
